docs.text: metamorph 🔬 An awesome metagenomic and metatranscriptomics pipeline This is the home of the pipeline, metamorph. Its long-term goals: to provide accurate quantification, taxonomic classification, and functional profiling of assembled (bacteria and archaea) metagenomes! Overview ¶ Welcome to metamorph's documentation! This guide is the main source of documentation for users that are getting started with the long pipeline name . The ./metamorph pipeline is composed several inter-related sub commands to setup and run the pipeline across different systems. Each of the available sub commands perform different functions: metamorph run Run the metamorph pipeline with your input files. metamorph unlock Unlocks a previous runs output directory. metamorph install Download remote reference files locally. metamorph cache Cache remote software containers locally. metamorph is a comprehensive workflow that starts off with assembly of short read DNA sequencing data (metagenome) to build contigs for each individual sample, followed by contig binning. Good quality genomic bins from all samples are futher combined and dereplicated to generate representative metagenome-assembled genomes or MAGs. These MAGs are further classified, quantified, and used to predict functional profiles. The short read DNA sequencing data (metatranscriptome) mapping to MAGs is used for functional profiling. It relies on technologies like Singularity 1 to maintain the highest-level of reproducibility. The pipeline consists of a series of data processing and quality-control steps orchestrated by Snakemake 2 , a flexible and scalable workflow management system, to submit jobs to a cluster. The pipeline is compatible with data generated from Illumina short-read sequencing technologies. As input, it accepts a set of FastQ files and can be run locally on a compute instance or on-premise using a cluster. A user can define the method or mode of execution. The pipeline can submit jobs to a cluster using a job scheduler like SLURM (more coming soon!). A hybrid approach ensures the pipeline is accessible to all users. Before getting started, we highly recommend reading through the usage section of each available sub command. For more information about issues or trouble-shooting a problem, please checkout our FAQ prior to opening an issue on Github . We encourage you to contribute new content and make improvements to existing content via pull request to our GitHub repository . docs.text: Walkthrough ¶ 1. About ¶ This page walks through setting up and running metamorph end-to-end using a small, public, real paired-end sequencing dataset, so you can see what each --workflow mode actually does before pointing the pipeline at your own data. If you haven't already, read the Introduction first — it explains why the pipeline is structured the way it is; this page focuses on doing . We'll use two tiny paired-end FASTQ samples from the nf-core/test-datasets mag branch. They're real assembled-metagenome reads with a small fraction of human (hg38) reads spiked in, which is exactly what makes them useful here — they're small enough to run in minutes, but large enough to exercise metamorph's host-removal step, not just skip it. 2. Prerequisites ¶ # Grab an interactive node — do not run on the head node! srun -N 1 -n 1 --time = 1 :00:00 --mem = 8gb --cpus-per-task = 4 --pty bash module purge module load singularity snakemake If you're running outside of a cluster that already hosts metamorph's reference bundle (e.g. off of NIH's Biowulf), also see metamorph install for pulling the reference bundle, and metamorph cache for pre-fetching containers into a shared, offline --sif-cache . 3. Getting a small, public test dataset ¶ mkdir -p /data/ $USER /metamorph_test/fastqs cd /data/ $USER /metamorph_test/fastqs BASE = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/test-datasets/mag/test_data" for f in test_minigut_hg38host_R1.fastq.gz test_minigut_hg38host_R2.fastq.gz \ test_minigut_sample2_hg38host_R1.fastq.gz test_minigut_sample2_hg38host_R2.fastq.gz ; do curl -sL -o " $f " " ${ BASE } / ${ f } " done This gives you two DNA samples: Sample Read pairs Compressed size (R1 + R2) test_minigut_hg38host 51,000 ~6.9 MB test_minigut_sample2_hg38host 25,993 ~3.6 MB 4. Building a sample sheet ¶ metamorph's sample sheet is a plain delimited text file with one column per data type ( DNA , and optionally RNA ), listing the R1/R2 paths for every sample — see metamorph run for the full format reference. This dataset is DNA-only, so it's a single DNA column: samplesheet.tsv DNA /data/$USER/metamorph_test/fastqs/test_minigut_hg38host_R1.fastq.gz /data/$USER/metamorph_test/fastqs/test_minigut_hg38host_R2.fastq.gz /data/$USER/metamorph_test/fastqs/test_minigut_sample2_hg38host_R1.fastq.gz /data/$USER/metamorph_test/fastqs/test_minigut_sample2_hg38host_R2.fastq.gz Tip .tsv / .txt sample sheets are tab-delimited; .csv sample sheets are comma-delimited. Paths must be absolute. 5. Dry-run the pipeline ¶ Before running anything for real, --dry-run shows you the exact DAG of jobs metamorph will build from your sample sheet, without executing a single one: ./metamorph run \ --samplesheet /data/ $USER /metamorph_test/samplesheet.tsv \ --output /data/ $USER /metamorph_test/output \ --mode local \ --sif-cache /data/OpenOmics/SIFs \ --dry-run --mode local runs everything serially on the current machine instead of submitting to SLURM — this is what makes it practical to iterate on a test dataset like this one from an interactive node. Swap in --mode slurm (the default) once you're ready to run at scale on your own data. 6. Walking through each mode of execution ¶ metamorph's --workflow flag controls how far the DAG extends past initial QC. All four modes below were generated from the same sample sheet above — only --workflow changes. 6.1 pre-screen (default) ¶ ./metamorph run --samplesheet samplesheet.tsv --output output_prescreen \ --mode local --workflow pre-screen --sif-cache /data/OpenOmics/SIFs --dry-run pre-screen performs quality control, host-read removal, and taxonomic pre-screening with Centrifuger. For our 2-sample sheet this resolves to: job count ----------------------------- ------- all 1 bowtie2_dehost 2 dna_centrifuger 2 metawrap_read_qc_skipBmtagger 2 total 7 Per sample, that's three real steps chained together: metawrap_read_qc_skipBmtagger — trims adapters and low-quality bases (Trim-Galore/Cutadapt via metaWRAP's read_qc module) and runs FastQC before/after trimming. bowtie2_dehost — aligns trimmed reads to the hg38 host genome and keeps only the read pairs where neither mate mapped, removing host contamination. This is the step that specifically needs the hg38-spiked reads in our test set to do anything meaningful — a purely microbial test file would pass through this step with (almost) nothing removed. dna_centrifuger — classifies the dehosted reads taxonomically against a GTDB+RefSeq index, producing a per-sample classification and quantification report. This is the cheapest, fastest mode, and a good default for "does my data look reasonable" checks before committing to the more expensive modes below. 6.2 read-based ¶ ./metamorph run --samplesheet samplesheet.tsv --output output_readbased \ --mode local --workflow read-based --sif-cache /data/OpenOmics/SIFs --dry-run read-based runs everything in pre-screen , then adds functional and taxonomic profiling on the same dehosted reads using HUMAnN3/MetaPhlAn4: job count -------------------------------- ------- all 1 bowtie2_dehost 2 dna_centrifuger 2 dna_humann_classify 2 dna_humann_diversity_calculation 1 dna_humann_summarize 1 metawrap_read_qc_skipBmtagger 2 total 11 dna_humann_classify runs per sample; dna_humann_diversity_calculation and dna_humann_summarize each run once across all samples in the sheet — they merge per-sample gene family/pathway abundance tables and compute diversity metrics (Shannon, richness, Jaccard, UniFrac), which is why those two only appear once regardless of sample count. Use --shallow-profile here if you want to skip HUMAnN3's translated-search step for a faster (if less sensitive) run. 6.3 assembly-based ¶ ./metamorph run --samplesheet samplesheet.tsv --output output_assembly \ --mode local --workflow assembly-based --sif-cache /data/OpenOmics/SIFs --dry-run assembly-based skips HUMAnN3/MetaPhlAn4 entirely and instead assembles, bins, and dereplicates each sample's dehosted reads into candidate genomes: job count ----------------------------- ------- all 1 bbtools_index_map 2 bin_stats 2 bowtie2_dehost 2 contig_annotation 1 cumulative_bin_stats 1 derep_bins 1 dna_centrifuger 2 dna_decompress_dehost_reads 2 gtdbtk_classify 1 gunc_detection 1 metawrap_binning 2 metawrap_genome_assembly 2 metawrap_read_qc_skipBmtagger 2 prep_genome_info 1 total 23 This is the most expensive of the four modes, and the job count more than triples versus pre-screen . Notably: dna_decompress_dehost_reads reappears here (and only here) — MEGAHIT/metaSPAdes, run inside metawrap_genome_assembly , need uncompressed FASTQ, so metamorph decompresses the dehosted .fastq.gz reads specifically for this mode rather than keeping every intermediate file uncompressed by default. metawrap_genome_assembly runs per sample (MEGAHIT and/or metaSPAdes, selectable via --assembler ), followed by per-sample metawrap_binning (MetaBAT2, MaxBin2, and metaWRAP's own consensus binner). derep_bins , prep_genome_info , gtdbtk_classify , gunc_detection , contig_annotation , and cumulative_bin_stats each run once across the whole cohort — dereplication (dRep) and taxonomic classification (GTDB-Tk) only make sense evaluated across all samples' bins together, which is also why the job count for these doesn't scale with sample count the way per-sample steps do. 6.4 combined ¶ ./metamorph run --samplesheet samplesheet.tsv --output output_combined \ --mode local --workflow combined --sif-cache /data/OpenOmics/SIFs --dry-run combined is the union of all three modes above — pre-screening, read-based profiling, and assembly-based binning, in one DAG: job count -------------------------------- ------- all 1 bbtools_index_map 2 bin_stats 2 bowtie2_dehost 2 contig_annotation 1 cumulative_bin_stats 1 derep_bins 1 dna_centrifuger 2 dna_decompress_dehost_reads 2 dna_humann_classify 2 dna_humann_diversity_calculation 1 dna_humann_summarize 1 gtdbtk_classify 1 gunc_detection 1 metawrap_binning 2 metawrap_genome_assembly 2 metawrap_read_qc_skipBmtagger 2 prep_genome_info 1 total 27 Each of the shared upstream steps ( metawrap_read_qc_skipBmtagger , bowtie2_dehost ) is computed exactly once and reused by both the read-based and assembly-based branches — Snakemake's DAG deduplicates on output file, so choosing combined over running read-based and assembly-based separately saves the cost of redoing QC and dehosting twice. About this environment The dehosting and classification steps above depend on reference indices (hg38 Bowtie2/STAR indices, a GTDB+RefSeq Centrifuger index, HUMAnN3/MetaPhlAn4/GTDB-Tk/GUNC databases) that live outside the pipeline's source code. On Biowulf these are already in place; elsewhere, run metamorph install first. Everything shown above is a --dry-run , so it reflects the job graph metamorph would execute — drop --dry-run once your reference bundle is in place to actually run it. 7. Inspecting the output directory ¶ Regardless of mode, --output is a self-contained Snakemake working directory. After a run you'll find: config.json — the fully-resolved configuration generated from your sample sheet and CLI flags. Worth reading if a run behaves unexpectedly. metagenome_results/metawrap_read_qc_skipBmtagger/<sample>/ — pre/post-trim FastQC reports. metagenome_results/trimmed_reads/<sample>/ — trimmed and dehosted FASTQ. metagenome_results/centrifuger_dna/ — taxonomic classification/quantification tables. metagenome_results/humann3_dna/ ( read-based / combined only) — gene family, pathway abundance/coverage, and diversity tables. metagenome_results/mags/ ( assembly-based / combined only) — dereplicated, taxonomically classified metagenome-assembled genomes and their per-sample statistics. 8. Re-running and cleaning up ¶ If a run is interrupted (killed job, cancelled allocation), Snakemake leaves the output directory locked. Use metamorph unlock before resubmitting to the same --output directory: ./metamorph unlock --output /data/ $USER /metamorph_test/output Because rule outputs are content-addressed by path, simply re-running the same metamorph run command afterward resumes from wherever the pipeline left off — completed samples/steps are not redone.

docs.text: Introduction ¶ 1. About ¶ This page is a conceptual introduction to metamorph. It is meant to be read before the command usage pages or the walkthrough — it explains why the pipeline is built the way it is, rather than how to invoke any one sub command. metamorph orchestrates a long chain of specialized, mostly decades-old bioinformatics tools (Trim-Galore, FastQC, Bowtie2/STAR, metaWRAP, MEGAHIT/metaSPAdes, MetaBAT2/MaxBin2, dRep, GTDB-Tk, GUNC, Centrifuger, HUMAnN3, MetaPhlAn4) behind a single, consistent interface. None of those tools were designed to interoperate, and metagenomics/metatranscriptomics data has properties that make gluing them together harder than a typical single-sample, single-reference genomics pipeline. Understanding those properties up front makes the rest of the documentation, and the pipeline's design choices, much easier to follow. 2. Portability ¶ metamorph is designed to run unmodified on very different systems: a shared HPC cluster with a SLURM scheduler and a site-wide reference bundle, a single workstation with no scheduler at all, and (eventually) other cluster backends. A few design decisions make that possible: Containers, not modules. Every rule that shells out to third-party software ( containerized: / singularity: in the Snakemake rules) runs inside a Singularity container pulled from a pinned image tag. This means the pipeline does not depend on whatever version of bowtie2 , metaspades , or humann3 happens to be installed on a given system, and a result produced on one cluster is reproducible on another. See metamorph cache for pre-fetching those containers into a shared, offline SIF cache — useful for avoiding DockerHub rate limits and for air-gapped systems. A pluggable execution backend. metamorph run --mode {slurm,local} swaps the orchestration layer without changing a single rule. slurm submits each job through sbatch for distributed execution; local runs the same DAG serially on one machine, which is what makes it practical to test the pipeline on a laptop or an interactive node with the tiny FASTQ files described in the walkthrough . Externalized reference data. Large reference databases (host genome indices, GTDB/RefSeq taxonomy databases, HUMAnN3/MetaPhlAn4 databases) are never bundled with the pipeline's source code — they are pulled once with metamorph install into a --resource-bundle / hardcoded reference path. On systems that already host a copy (e.g. NIH's Biowulf), users skip this step entirely. A generated, self-describing config. The run sub command resolves the sample sheet, CLI flags, and the JSON files under config/ into a single config.json written into the output directory. That output directory is a complete, standalone Snakemake working directory — it can be linted, resumed, or unlocked ( metamorph unlock ) independently of the code that generated it. Portability is what lets the same sample sheet and the same metamorph run invocation produce the same directed acyclic graph of jobs whether it's submitted to a thousand-node cluster or dry-run on a single core. 3. Why metagenomics/metatranscriptomics needs a pipeline like this ¶ A handful of properties specific to metagenomic and metatranscriptomic data make this domain notably harder to build a portable, reproducible pipeline for than single-organism, single-reference sequencing analysis: There is no single reference genome. A human or mouse pipeline can align every read to one reference. A metagenome is an unknown mixture of many, often uncharacterized, organisms. metamorph never assumes a reference — it assembles each sample de novo (MEGAHIT and/or metaSPAdes, selectable via --assembler ), bins the resulting contigs into candidate genomes (MetaBAT2, MaxBin2, and metaWRAP's consensus binning), and only then classifies and dereplicates ("MAGs") — a fundamentally different, and much more compute-intensive, path than reference-based alignment. Host contamination has to be actively removed, not just ignored. Stool, tissue, and most other sample types contain host DNA/RNA alongside the microbial signal of interest. If it isn't removed, host reads can dominate assemblies, waste compute, and are a re-identification/privacy risk when host is human. Every DNA and RNA sample pair in metamorph passes through an explicit dehosting step ( bowtie2_dehost for DNA against hg38, STAR-based dehosting for RNA) before anything taxonomic or functional is computed downstream. The tools involved have inconsistent, sometimes contradictory input expectations. metaWRAP's read_qc module, for example, only accepts uncompressed FASTQ, while every other stage in the pipeline standardizes on gzip-compressed FASTQ to keep the working directory's storage footprint manageable. metamorph absorbs that inconsistency internally (decompressing on the way in, recompressing the trimmed output on the way out) so it never leaks into the sample sheet or the user-facing interface. Multiply this kind of quirk across a dozen tools and the value of centralizing it in one maintained pipeline, instead of every user re-solving it themselves, becomes clear. Reference databases are enormous and shared, not per-sample. Host indices, GTDB-Tk's taxonomy database, and Centrifuger/HUMAnN3/MetaPhlAn4's classification databases are commonly hundreds of gigabytes, far larger than any individual FASTQ input. These are treated as external, site-provided resources ( metamorph install ) rather than pipeline inputs, so that a run's cost scales with sample size, not with the size of the reference collection it's compared against. Multi-omic sample pairing is optional but load-bearing when present. A project may contain DNA only, or matched DNA + RNA per subject. When RNA is present, metamorph pairs it with its corresponding DNA sample throughout the assembly-based workflow so functional profiling (HUMAnN3) and MAG-level RNA mapping are computed against the same subject's assembled genomes — not a generic reference — which is what makes the metatranscriptomic results interpretable at all. Runtime and resource needs vary by two orders of magnitude across stages. Read QC and dehosting finish in minutes; genome assembly, binning, and dereplication can take hours to days and need substantially more memory. The --workflow {pre-screen,read-based,assembly-based,combined} switch exists specifically so users can stop after the cheap, fast stages ( pre-screen ) when that's all a project needs, rather than always paying for the most expensive stages. The rest of the manual and the walkthrough build on these ideas concretely — showing what actually gets produced at each stage, using a small, public, real dataset.

docs.text: Vignette: ZymoBIOMICS Microbial Community DNA Standard (D6305/D6306) ¶ Status Every number and figure on this page comes from a real, completed metamorph --workflow combined run against 2 samples ( in3634_1 = D6305, in3634_2 = D6306). This page is deliberately standalone and does not compare any number to the D6300 vignette 's results — different product format, different sample count, different sequencing run, no statistical pooling between the two pages. Section 6 spells out exactly how and why. 1. About ¶ ZymoBIOMICS® Microbial Community DNA Standard (catalog D6305 , 200 ng; D6306 , 2,000 ng) ships the same defined 8-bacteria/2-yeast community as the D6300 Microbial Community Standard already covered on this site — but as pre-extracted, purified genomic DNA , not live/fixed cells. The vendor's own datasheet ( DS1706 ) covers both products: page 1 is D6300 (the cellular standard, 10 preps); page 2 is the DNA standard, sold at two input masses, D6305 (200 ng) and D6306 (2,000 ng) — D6305 and D6306 are the same product at two masses, not two different compositions. Its defined target composition is the same evenly-balanced mix as D6300's Table 1 (12% genomic DNA per bacterium, 2% per yeast) — confirmed directly, since the public datasheet's own DNA-standard page gives no per-species numeric table, only an unlabeled composition chart with the same 10-organism legend. Because no extraction step happens on the user's end at all — the DNA arrives already purified — this standard isolates everything downstream of extraction: library preparation, sequencing, and classification bias, with extraction-method bias specifically removed as a variable. That is a different, narrower question than the D6300 page asks (which includes extraction bias), which is the main reason this page keeps its own analysis rather than folding into the existing one. 2. Vendor ground truth ¶ Same 10 organisms, same defined mix as the D6300 page's Table 1 — reused here unchanged, renormalized across the 8 target bacteria to the same Genome Copy % basis (the correct target for shotgun-sequencing-derived abundance, per that page's Section 2 note; genome sizes are for the same strains either way): Species Genome Copy % (target, renormalized across 8 bacteria) Lactobacillus fermentum 21.84 Staphylococcus aureus 15.37 Enterococcus faecalis 14.76 Listeria monocytogenes 14.05 Bacillus subtilis 10.41 Salmonella enterica 8.80 Escherichia coli 8.59 Pseudomonas aeruginosa 6.17 3. Data used in this run ¶ in3634_1 in3634_2 Product D6305 D6306 DNA input mass 200 ng 2,000 ng Raw read pairs 5,356,541 5,928,215 Sequencer MiniSeq (run date 2023-01-23, per the submitter's rawdata-links manifest) same --host-genome used No No Standard material (D6305/D6306) was obtained directly from Zymo as the distributor; sequencing itself was performed via a third-party core facility, per the submitted rawdata-links manifest. This run used metamorph's combined workflow with no --host-genome yeast references injected — unlike the D6300 page, any yeast signal here was never screened out before classification, so both methods below can and do detect yeast reads directly. Per-sample QC, from metamorph's own qc_summary.tsv (see the D6300 page's Section 4.2 for the dehosting methodology it reuses): Metric in3634_1 (D6305) in3634_2 (D6306) Post-trim read pairs 5,348,510 (99.85%) 5,919,733 (99.86%) Post-hg38-dehost read pairs 5,343,788 (99.91% of post-trim) 5,914,209 (99.91% of post-trim) hg38 host alignment 0.0883% 0.0933% Classifier input fragments 5,343,788 5,914,209 Classified (Centrifuger) 96.02% 96.18% — bacterial 92.44% 92.60% — eukaryotic (yeast + noise) 2.30% 2.31% Unclassified 3.97% 3.81% QC flags raised none none Both samples are roughly a third of the per-replicate depth of the D6300 page's 7 ENA replicates (14–19M read pairs there vs. ~5.3–5.9M here) — one more reason this page's numbers aren't pooled with that page's. 4. Methodology: two independent estimates, same generic rules as the D6300 page ¶ This page reuses the same two generic, mechanical naming rules established on the D6300 page ( Section 5 ) — GTDB placeholder-suffix collapse, and current-GTDB-name mapping for B. subtilis / spizizenii and L. fermentum / Limosilactobacillus — applied identically here, no new rules invented for this data. Read-based : Centrifuger's per-sample species-level abundance ( centrifuger_dna/<sample>_centrifuger_quantification_report.tsv ), same as the D6300 page's read-based method. Assembly-based : this run's own --workflow combined output, built entirely from metaWRAP — metawrap_binning / metawrap_bin_refine (assembly, binning, bin refinement), metawrap_bin_refine/dRep/dereplicated_genomes/ (the dereplicated genome set), metawrap_kmer/GTDBTK_classify_wf/gtdbtk.bac120.summary.tsv (genome identity), and mags/<sample>/DNA/<sample>.refstats (each sample's reads mapped back against that set) — same coverage-normalization logic as the D6300 page's assembly-based method (recruited bases ÷ genome size). Two bins metaWRAP's own QC rejected were hand-rescued — see Section 5.1 for exactly why, and why one is reported as its own species while the other is reported as a combined, unseparated pair rather than either individual species. The assembly-based estimate covers all 8 bacteria, but 2 of them only as one combined category With only 2 samples, this run's own metaWRAP/dRep dereplication recovered genomes for just 5 of the 8 target bacteria outright ( metawrap_bin_refine/dRep/dRep.SMALL_BINSET_WARNING is present in the output). E. faecalis was added by hand as its own species after confirming its rejected bin was real, uncontaminated sequence that only failed on completeness (Section 5.1). E. coli and Salmonella enterica were also added by hand, but as a single combined category — their only candidate bin is a genuine two-organism mixture that cannot be split into two per-species numbers (Section 5.1) — compared against the sum of both organisms' individual vendor targets, not either one's target alone. The result is 7 categories (6 individual species + 1 combined pair) that together cover the full 8-bacteria target basis with no artificial exclusion — in the figure (Section 5), the combined category is drawn as alternating stripes of E. coli 's and Salmonella 's own colors, never as a solid fill, so it's never mistaken for either species individually or for a true zero. n = 1 per product (D6305 and D6306 are two different input masses of the same standard, not replicates of each other) — no standard deviation or significance test is computed anywhere on this page; both samples' values are reported individually. 5. Results ¶ Read-based (Centrifuger, all 8 bacteria): Species Target % D6305 read-based % fold D6306 read-based % fold Lactobacillus fermentum 21.84 29.04 1.33× 29.74 1.36× Staphylococcus aureus 15.37 15.23 0.99× 14.90 0.97× Enterococcus faecalis 14.76 10.01 0.68× 9.72 0.66× Listeria monocytogenes 14.05 18.25 1.30× 18.01 1.28× Bacillus subtilis 10.41 14.62 1.40× 14.64 1.41× Salmonella enterica 8.80 6.06 0.69× 6.04 0.69× Escherichia coli 8.59 2.23 0.26× 2.17 0.25× Pseudomonas aeruginosa 6.17 4.57 0.74× 4.78 0.77× Assembly-based (this run's own metaWRAP/dRep/GTDB-Tk output — target renormalized across the full 8-bacteria basis, same as the read-based table above, since the combined category below accounts for the remaining 2 species' mass): Species / category Target % D6305 assembly-based % fold D6306 assembly-based % fold Lactobacillus fermentum 21.84 21.71 0.99× 22.16 1.01× Enterococcus faecalis 14.76 20.29 1.37× 20.05 1.36× Staphylococcus aureus 15.37 17.80 1.16× 17.39 1.13× Listeria monocytogenes 14.05 16.72 1.19× 16.51 1.17× E. coli + S. enterica (combined, not separable) 17.39 8.35 0.48× 8.51 0.49× Bacillus subtilis 10.41 10.44 1.00× 10.42 1.00× Pseudomonas aeruginosa 6.17 4.69 0.76× 4.96 0.80× See Section 5.1 for exactly how E. faecalis was recovered as its own species, and why E. coli / S. enterica are reported together instead. The striped segment in the assembly-based bars above (alternating E. coli 's and Salmonella 's own colors) is a real measurement — metamorph recovered their combined genomic mass — but it is not a per-species number for either organism; it's compared against the sum of both organisms' individual targets, never against either one alone. Yeasts (reported raw, not renormalized across the 8 bacteria, matching the D6300 page's convention — both are left unscreened here since --host-genome wasn't used): D6305 read-based D6306 read-based Saccharomyces cerevisiae 0.4408% 0.4325% Cryptococcus neoformans 0.0000% 0.0000% 5.1 Why E. coli / Salmonella only have a number together, and why E. faecalis has its own ¶ metaWRAP's bin_refinement step keeps a bin only if it clears completeness ≥50% and contamination ≤5%. Checking the bins it rejected ( metawrap_binning/<sample>/{metabat2,maxbin2}_bins.stats , before refinement) shows two different failure modes, not one: A genuine two-organism chimera for E. coli / Salmonella enterica . MetaBAT2 placed both into a single bin per sample, flagged by CheckM's own lineage call as Enterobacteriaceae (the family both belong to) at 91–99% completeness but 86–98% contamination . Mapping that bin against the vendor's reference genomes with Mash confirms it's a real mixture, not noise from an unrelated organism — it sits almost exactly equidistant between the E. coli and Salmonella references (distance 0.0194 vs. 0.0199). MaxBin2 did better, mostly separating them into an E. coli -dominant bin (0.0186 vs. 0.0706 to the two references) and a Salmonella -dominant bin (0.0150 vs. 0.0525) — but each still carried 10.6% and 37.3% contamination respectively, both well past the 5% ceiling. Every candidate bin for either organism, from either binner, fails refinement — there is no single-organism bin for dRep to ever see, and no honest way to split a chimeric bin's coverage between two species without inventing a per-contig classification step metaWRAP/metamorph never performs. What is honest to report : the chimeric bin's total coverage, since it genuinely represents both organisms' combined genomic mass — just not divisible between them. The best candidate ( in3634_2_bin.9 , 99.27% complete, 9.12 Mb — close to the sum of the two real genomes, ~4.9 + 4.8 Mb, consistent with holding near-complete copies of both) was added by hand to the mapping index as one combined category , reported against the sum of both organisms' vendor targets. A real but incomplete genome for E. faecalis . A bin in each sample ( in3634_1_bin.2 , in3634_2_bin.8 ) is zero contamination and, per Mash, clearly real E. faecalis sequence (distance 0.034, far closer than any other reference genome) — it failed refinement only on completeness (35–41% of expected marker genes, below the 50% floor). Since there's no mixing problem here, this bin was added by hand as its own species, compared against its own individual target. Both rescued bins were added to the same combined 7-genome mapping index (the 5 real dRep winners + these 2) and both samples' reads were remapped against it with the exact same bbsplit.sh invocation and parameters metamorph's own bbtools_index_map rule uses ( minid=0.90 , sortscafs=f , nzo=f ) — the assembly-based table above includes the result. This is why the category that only exists in combined form is specifically E. coli + Salmonella — the same two organisms the D6300 page's own Mash heatmap (reused below) already flags as the most genomically similar pair in the entire 10-genome standard by a wide margin: E. coli / Salmonella enterica sit at 0.16 — the closest pair anywhere in this heatmap, well below the next-closest bacterial pair (0.20) — which is exactly the kind of genomic similarity that defeats composition-and-coverage-based binning (MetaBAT2, MaxBin2) regardless of how much data goes in. This is the same heatmap and finding documented in the D6300 page's Section 7.1 ; nothing about it is specific to this page's data — it's a property of the reference genomes themselves, which is exactly why the same two organisms fail to separate here too, in a completely different, shallower, independently-sequenced run. Both rescues are hand-built additions, not something metamorph run itself produces Section 7's claim that this page uses no external tools refers to parameters and binaries (same bbsplit.sh , same flags as metamorph's own rule) — but the decision to add bins metaWRAP's own QC rejected, and remap reads against them, is an analysis-script judgment call made for this page, not pipeline behavior. A real metamorph run on this data would stop at 5 recovered genomes, exactly as dRep /GTDB-Tk's output already shows. The combined E. coli / Salmonella category in particular is not a claim that metamorph detected and distinguished both organisms — it's the opposite: a documented, honest statement that it couldn't, with the one number it legitimately could produce (their total) reported instead of silence or a wrong split. What this independently corroborates (and doesn't) ¶ Of the 7 categories this run's own assembly-based method can now speak to, one reproduces the D6300 page's central finding directly: Bacillus subtilis : read-based over-calls it clearly (1.40–1.41× target, both samples), while this run's own assembly-based estimate lands almost exactly on target instead (1.00×, both samples) — a read-based-vs-assembly-based divergence for the same organism, in the same direction, as the D6300 page's Section 6 (read-based 1.31× there, assembly-based not significantly different from target). This is independent evidence for the same read-based-classifier-specific effect — from a different extraction method (none, in this case), different sequencing run, different year, and about a third of the per-sample depth. E. coli* + Salmonella enterica , combined : read-based's two individual under-calls (0.25–0.26× and 0.69×) sum to a combined measured share well below the two organisms' combined target — and the assembly-based combined category lands at 0.48–0.49× target too, the same direction. This is the closest this page can get to the D6300 page's finding that read-based disagrees in direction with genome-level methods for these two specifically (there, genome-level over-called both; here, the combined genome-level number still under-calls, same direction as read-based) — a genuinely different outcome from the D6300 page, not a replication, and impossible to resolve further on this page since the two organisms were never separable here to begin with (Section 5.1). Enterococcus faecalis : read-based under-calls it (0.66–0.68×) while this page's rescued assembly-based estimate over -calls it instead (1.36–1.37×) — the two methods disagree in direction, which doesn't match the D6300 page's shape for this organism (there, assembly-based was also under target, 0.58×, diagnosed as a near-duplicate-dRep-cluster artifact that doesn't apply here at all, since this run never had two competing E. faecalis clusters). This page's own number carries its own caveat (Section 5.1): coverage computed from an incomplete bin likely skews high, since assembly tends to preferentially capture an organism's higher-coverage regions first — some or all of the 1.36–1.37× over-call may be that bias rather than a real difference from read-based. Lactobacillus fermentum : over-called by read-based here too (1.33–1.36×), but assembly-based lands almost exactly on target instead (0.99–1.01×) — on the D6300 page both methods over-called it (2.11× and 1.55×) and agreed on direction. Does not replicate the D6300 page's shape. Staphylococcus aureus* and *Listeria monocytogenes : both methods over-call by broadly similar margins here (1.13–1.16× and 1.17–1.30×, respectively) — neither the dramatic S. aureus under-call (0.19–0.23× on the D6300 page) nor any particular Listeria pattern reproduces here. Pseudomonas aeruginosa : both methods under-call it by similar margins here (0.69–0.81×) — a different shape from the D6300 page, where read-based and assembly-based were both close to or slightly over target. With n=1 per condition and no formal significance test anywhere on this page, every comparison above is a pattern match, not a statistical claim — flagged as such, not overstated. 6. Caveats and how this differs from the D6300 vignette ¶ No replication. D6305 and D6306 are one sample each, not biological or technical replicates of each other — there is no SD, no t -test, and no convergence analysis anywhere on this page, unlike every quantitative claim on the D6300 page. No --host-genome yeast screening. Yeast reads were never removed before classification here, so read-based classification detects real (if small) S. cerevisiae signal (~0.43%) — not comparable to the D6300 page's near-zero yeast numbers, which reflect those reads being screened out before any classifier saw them, not a true absence. Cryptococcus neoformans is undetected by read-based here regardless (0.0000% both samples). Lower depth, different run, different year. ~5.3–5.9M read pairs per sample here vs. 14–19M on the D6300 page; different sequencing instrument/run, sequenced via a third-party core rather than the public ENA deposition the D6300 page uses. The in-run assembly-based estimate covers all 8 bacteria, but 2 of those 8 ( E. coli , Salmonella ) only as one combined, unseparated category, and both additions beyond the pipeline's own 5 are hand-rescued bins, not pipeline output. metaWRAP/dRep/GTDB-Tk recovered 5 genomes outright ( SMALL_BINSET_WARNING , Section 4); E. faecalis and the E. coli / Salmonella chimera were both added by hand after confirming via Mash what each rejected bin actually was (Section 5.1) — a judgment call made for this page, not something metamorph run itself would do. There is no second, independent genome-level method on this page (unlike the D6300 page's reference-mapping cross-check) that could split the chimeric bin into two per-species numbers — the combined category is the ceiling of what's recoverable here, not a limitation of the write-up. D6305 vs. D6306 look like the same measured composition. Every species' read-based % is within about half a percentage point between the two masses, and the two samples' assembly-based numbers (for the 5 recovered species) agree just as closely — consistent with both being the same purified-DNA mixture, just more or less of it. The vendor's own datasheet suggests input mass mainly affects downstream PCR chimera formation and GC bias in library prep, not composition at the DNA level directly; nothing in this run's results contradicts that, but this run never varied PCR cycle count to test it directly. 7. Reproducing this page ¶ Samples in3634_1 (D6305, 200 ng) and in3634_2 (D6306, 2,000 ng) are internal, not public — reproduction requires the vendor's DNA standard (D6305/D6306, see the product datasheet ) processed through the same metamorph run --workflow combined invocation used for the D6300 page (Section 3 there), minus --host-genome . The read-based numbers and the 5 pipeline-native assembly-based genomes come directly out of that one invocation's metagenome_results/ ; the other 2 categories ( E. faecalis , and the combined E. coli / Salmonella pair — Section 5.1) each required one additional manual bbsplit.sh run (same binary/parameters as metamorph's own bbtools_index_map rule) against a hand-built 7-genome reference set — not something metamorph run produces on its own. Analysis scripts: docs/manual/zymo_vignette_scripts/zymo_d6305_d6306_analysis.py (read-based), zymo_d6305_d6306_assembly_analysis.py (assembly-based, all 8 bacteria via 7 categories, reads the rescued-genome mapping from d6305_d6306_asm7_mags/ ), build_d6305_d6306_chart.py (figure). The two rescued bins' remapping output is persisted at docs/manual/zymo_vignette_scripts/d6305_d6306_asm7_mags/{in3634_1,in3634_2}.refstats .

docs.text: ZymoBIOMICS® Microbial Community DNA Standard (catalog D6305 , 200 ng; D6306 , 2,000 ng) ships the same defined 8-bacteria/2-yeast community as the D6300 Microbial Community Standard already covered on this site — but as pre-extracted, purified genomic DNA , not live/fixed cells. The vendor's own datasheet ( DS1706 ) covers both products: page 1 is D6300 (the cellular standard, 10 preps); page 2 is the DNA standard, sold at two input masses, D6305 (200 ng) and D6306 (2,000 ng) — D6305 and D6306 are the same product at two masses, not two different compositions. Its defined target composition is the same evenly-balanced mix as D6300's Table 1 (12% genomic DNA per bacterium, 2% per yeast) — confirmed directly, since the public datasheet's own DNA-standard page gives no per-species numeric table, only an unlabeled composition chart with the same 10-organism legend. Because no extraction step happens on the user's end at all — the DNA arrives already purified — this standard isolates everything downstream of extraction: library preparation, sequencing, and classification bias, with extraction-method bias specifically removed as a variable. That is a different, narrower question than the D6300 page asks (which includes extraction bias), which is the main reason this page keeps its own analysis rather than folding into the existing one.

docs.text: This page reuses the same two generic, mechanical naming rules established on the D6300 page ( Section 5 ) — GTDB placeholder-suffix collapse, and current-GTDB-name mapping for B. subtilis / spizizenii and L. fermentum / Limosilactobacillus — applied identically here, no new rules invented for this data. Read-based : Centrifuger's per-sample species-level abundance ( centrifuger_dna/<sample>_centrifuger_quantification_report.tsv ), same as the D6300 page's read-based method. Assembly-based : this run's own --workflow combined output, built entirely from metaWRAP — metawrap_binning / metawrap_bin_refine (assembly, binning, bin refinement), metawrap_bin_refine/dRep/dereplicated_genomes/ (the dereplicated genome set), metawrap_kmer/GTDBTK_classify_wf/gtdbtk.bac120.summary.tsv (genome identity), and mags/<sample>/DNA/<sample>.refstats (each sample's reads mapped back against that set) — same coverage-normalization logic as the D6300 page's assembly-based method (recruited bases ÷ genome size). Two bins metaWRAP's own QC rejected were hand-rescued — see Section 5.1 for exactly why, and why one is reported as its own species while the other is reported as a combined, unseparated pair rather than either individual species. The assembly-based estimate covers all 8 bacteria, but 2 of them only as one combined category With only 2 samples, this run's own metaWRAP/dRep dereplication recovered genomes for just 5 of the 8 target bacteria outright ( metawrap_bin_refine/dRep/dRep.SMALL_BINSET_WARNING is present in the output). E. faecalis was added by hand as its own species after confirming its rejected bin was real, uncontaminated sequence that only failed on completeness (Section 5.1). E. coli and Salmonella enterica were also added by hand, but as a single combined category — their only candidate bin is a genuine two-organism mixture that cannot be split into two per-species numbers (Section 5.1) — compared against the sum of both organisms' individual vendor targets, not either one's target alone. The result is 7 categories (6 individual species + 1 combined pair) that together cover the full 8-bacteria target basis with no artificial exclusion — in the figure (Section 5), the combined category is drawn as alternating stripes of E. coli 's and Salmonella 's own colors, never as a solid fill, so it's never mistaken for either species individually or for a true zero. n = 1 per product (D6305 and D6306 are two different input masses of the same standard, not replicates of each other) — no standard deviation or significance test is computed anywhere on this page; both samples' values are reported individually.

docs.title: 5. Results

docs.text: metaWRAP's bin_refinement step keeps a bin only if it clears completeness ≥50% and contamination ≤5%. Checking the bins it rejected ( metawrap_binning/<sample>/{metabat2,maxbin2}_bins.stats , before refinement) shows two different failure modes, not one: A genuine two-organism chimera for E. coli / Salmonella enterica . MetaBAT2 placed both into a single bin per sample, flagged by CheckM's own lineage call as Enterobacteriaceae (the family both belong to) at 91–99% completeness but 86–98% contamination . Mapping that bin against the vendor's reference genomes with Mash confirms it's a real mixture, not noise from an unrelated organism — it sits almost exactly equidistant between the E. coli and Salmonella references (distance 0.0194 vs. 0.0199). MaxBin2 did better, mostly separating them into an E. coli -dominant bin (0.0186 vs. 0.0706 to the two references) and a Salmonella -dominant bin (0.0150 vs. 0.0525) — but each still carried 10.6% and 37.3% contamination respectively, both well past the 5% ceiling. Every candidate bin for either organism, from either binner, fails refinement — there is no single-organism bin for dRep to ever see, and no honest way to split a chimeric bin's coverage between two species without inventing a per-contig classification step metaWRAP/metamorph never performs. What is honest to report : the chimeric bin's total coverage, since it genuinely represents both organisms' combined genomic mass — just not divisible between them. The best candidate ( in3634_2_bin.9 , 99.27% complete, 9.12 Mb — close to the sum of the two real genomes, ~4.9 + 4.8 Mb, consistent with holding near-complete copies of both) was added by hand to the mapping index as one combined category , reported against the sum of both organisms' vendor targets. A real but incomplete genome for E. faecalis . A bin in each sample ( in3634_1_bin.2 , in3634_2_bin.8 ) is zero contamination and, per Mash, clearly real E. faecalis sequence (distance 0.034, far closer than any other reference genome) — it failed refinement only on completeness (35–41% of expected marker genes, below the 50% floor). Since there's no mixing problem here, this bin was added by hand as its own species, compared against its own individual target. Both rescued bins were added to the same combined 7-genome mapping index (the 5 real dRep winners + these 2) and both samples' reads were remapped against it with the exact same bbsplit.sh invocation and parameters metamorph's own bbtools_index_map rule uses ( minid=0.90 , sortscafs=f , nzo=f ) — the assembly-based table above includes the result. This is why the category that only exists in combined form is specifically E. coli + Salmonella — the same two organisms the D6300 page's own Mash heatmap (reused below) already flags as the most genomically similar pair in the entire 10-genome standard by a wide margin: E. coli / Salmonella enterica sit at 0.16 — the closest pair anywhere in this heatmap, well below the next-closest bacterial pair (0.20) — which is exactly the kind of genomic similarity that defeats composition-and-coverage-based binning (MetaBAT2, MaxBin2) regardless of how much data goes in. This is the same heatmap and finding documented in the D6300 page's Section 7.1 ; nothing about it is specific to this page's data — it's a property of the reference genomes themselves, which is exactly why the same two organisms fail to separate here too, in a completely different, shallower, independently-sequenced run. Both rescues are hand-built additions, not something metamorph run itself produces Section 7's claim that this page uses no external tools refers to parameters and binaries (same bbsplit.sh , same flags as metamorph's own rule) — but the decision to add bins metaWRAP's own QC rejected, and remap reads against them, is an analysis-script judgment call made for this page, not pipeline behavior. A real metamorph run on this data would stop at 5 recovered genomes, exactly as dRep /GTDB-Tk's output already shows. The combined E. coli / Salmonella category in particular is not a claim that metamorph detected and distinguished both organisms — it's the opposite: a documented, honest statement that it couldn't, with the one number it legitimately could produce (their total) reported instead of silence or a wrong split.
docs.title: 5.1 Why E. coli/Salmonella only have a number together, and why E. faecalis has its own

docs.text: Of the 7 categories this run's own assembly-based method can now speak to, one reproduces the D6300 page's central finding directly: Bacillus subtilis : read-based over-calls it clearly (1.40–1.41× target, both samples), while this run's own assembly-based estimate lands almost exactly on target instead (1.00×, both samples) — a read-based-vs-assembly-based divergence for the same organism, in the same direction, as the D6300 page's Section 6 (read-based 1.31× there, assembly-based not significantly different from target). This is independent evidence for the same read-based-classifier-specific effect — from a different extraction method (none, in this case), different sequencing run, different year, and about a third of the per-sample depth. E. coli* + Salmonella enterica , combined : read-based's two individual under-calls (0.25–0.26× and 0.69×) sum to a combined measured share well below the two organisms' combined target — and the assembly-based combined category lands at 0.48–0.49× target too, the same direction. This is the closest this page can get to the D6300 page's finding that read-based disagrees in direction with genome-level methods for these two specifically (there, genome-level over-called both; here, the combined genome-level number still under-calls, same direction as read-based) — a genuinely different outcome from the D6300 page, not a replication, and impossible to resolve further on this page since the two organisms were never separable here to begin with (Section 5.1). Enterococcus faecalis : read-based under-calls it (0.66–0.68×) while this page's rescued assembly-based estimate over -calls it instead (1.36–1.37×) — the two methods disagree in direction, which doesn't match the D6300 page's shape for this organism (there, assembly-based was also under target, 0.58×, diagnosed as a near-duplicate-dRep-cluster artifact that doesn't apply here at all, since this run never had two competing E. faecalis clusters). This page's own number carries its own caveat (Section 5.1): coverage computed from an incomplete bin likely skews high, since assembly tends to preferentially capture an organism's higher-coverage regions first — some or all of the 1.36–1.37× over-call may be that bias rather than a real difference from read-based. Lactobacillus fermentum : over-called by read-based here too (1.33–1.36×), but assembly-based lands almost exactly on target instead (0.99–1.01×) — on the D6300 page both methods over-called it (2.11× and 1.55×) and agreed on direction. Does not replicate the D6300 page's shape. Staphylococcus aureus* and *Listeria monocytogenes : both methods over-call by broadly similar margins here (1.13–1.16× and 1.17–1.30×, respectively) — neither the dramatic S. aureus under-call (0.19–0.23× on the D6300 page) nor any particular Listeria pattern reproduces here. Pseudomonas aeruginosa : both methods under-call it by similar margins here (0.69–0.81×) — a different shape from the D6300 page, where read-based and assembly-based were both close to or slightly over target. With n=1 per condition and no formal significance test anywhere on this page, every comparison above is a pattern match, not a statistical claim — flagged as such, not overstated.
docs.title: What this independently corroborates (and doesn't)

docs.text: No replication. D6305 and D6306 are one sample each, not biological or technical replicates of each other — there is no SD, no t -test, and no convergence analysis anywhere on this page, unlike every quantitative claim on the D6300 page. No --host-genome yeast screening. Yeast reads were never removed before classification here, so read-based classification detects real (if small) S. cerevisiae signal (~0.43%) — not comparable to the D6300 page's near-zero yeast numbers, which reflect those reads being screened out before any classifier saw them, not a true absence. Cryptococcus neoformans is undetected by read-based here regardless (0.0000% both samples). Lower depth, different run, different year. ~5.3–5.9M read pairs per sample here vs. 14–19M on the D6300 page; different sequencing instrument/run, sequenced via a third-party core rather than the public ENA deposition the D6300 page uses. The in-run assembly-based estimate covers all 8 bacteria, but 2 of those 8 ( E. coli , Salmonella ) only as one combined, unseparated category, and both additions beyond the pipeline's own 5 are hand-rescued bins, not pipeline output. metaWRAP/dRep/GTDB-Tk recovered 5 genomes outright ( SMALL_BINSET_WARNING , Section 4); E. faecalis and the E. coli / Salmonella chimera were both added by hand after confirming via Mash what each rejected bin actually was (Section 5.1) — a judgment call made for this page, not something metamorph run itself would do. There is no second, independent genome-level method on this page (unlike the D6300 page's reference-mapping cross-check) that could split the chimeric bin into two per-species numbers — the combined category is the ceiling of what's recoverable here, not a limitation of the write-up. D6305 vs. D6306 look like the same measured composition. Every species' read-based % is within about half a percentage point between the two masses, and the two samples' assembly-based numbers (for the 5 recovered species) agree just as closely — consistent with both being the same purified-DNA mixture, just more or less of it. The vendor's own datasheet suggests input mass mainly affects downstream PCR chimera formation and GC bias in library prep, not composition at the DNA level directly; nothing in this run's results contradicts that, but this run never varied PCR cycle count to test it directly.
docs.title: 6. Caveats and how this differs from the D6300 vignette

docs.text: Samples in3634_1 (D6305, 200 ng) and in3634_2 (D6306, 2,000 ng) are internal, not public — reproduction requires the vendor's DNA standard (D6305/D6306, see the product datasheet ) processed through the same metamorph run --workflow combined invocation used for the D6300 page (Section 3 there), minus --host-genome . The read-based numbers and the 5 pipeline-native assembly-based genomes come directly out of that one invocation's metagenome_results/ ; the other 2 categories ( E. faecalis , and the combined E. coli / Salmonella pair — Section 5.1) each required one additional manual bbsplit.sh run (same binary/parameters as metamorph's own bbtools_index_map rule) against a hand-built 7-genome reference set — not something metamorph run produces on its own. Analysis scripts: docs/manual/zymo_vignette_scripts/zymo_d6305_d6306_analysis.py (read-based), zymo_d6305_d6306_assembly_analysis.py (assembly-based, all 8 bacteria via 7 categories, reads the rescued-genome mapping from d6305_d6306_asm7_mags/ ), build_d6305_d6306_chart.py (figure). The two rescued bins' remapping output is persisted at docs/manual/zymo_vignette_scripts/d6305_d6306_asm7_mags/{in3634_1,in3634_2}.refstats .

docs.text: metamorph cache ¶ 1. About ¶ The metamorph executable is composed of several inter-related sub commands. Please see metamorph -h for all available options. This part of the documentation describes options and concepts for metamorph cache sub command in more detail. With minimal configuration, the cache sub command enables you to cache remote resources for the metamorph pipeline. Caching remote resources allows the pipeline to run in an offline mode. The cache sub command can also be used to pull our pre-built reference bundles onto a new cluster or target system. The cache sub command creates local cache on the filesysytem for resources hosted on DockerHub or AWS S3. These resources are normally pulled onto the filesystem when the pipeline runs; however, due to network issues or DockerHub pull rate limits, it may make sense to pull the resources once so a shared cache can be created and re-used. It is worth noting that a singularity cache cannot normally be shared across users. Singularity strictly enforces that its cache is owned by the user. To get around this issue, the cache subcommand can be used to create local SIFs on the filesystem from images on DockerHub. 2. Synopsis ¶ Coming Soon!

docs.text: metamorph run ¶ 1. About ¶ The metamorph executable is composed of several inter-related subcommands. Please see metamorph -h for all available options. This part of the documentation describes the options and concepts for the metamorph run sub-command in more detail. With minimal configuration, the run sub-command allows you to start running the metagenomics/metatranscriptomics pipeline. Setting up the metamorph pipeline is fast and easy! In its most basic form, metamorph run requires two arguments: A sample sheet provided with --samplesheet An output directory provided with --output 2. Synopsis ¶ $ metamorph run [--help] \ [--mode {slurm,local}] [--job-name JOB_NAME] \ [--master-job-node {norm,unlimited,quick}] \ [--triggers TRIGGER [TRIGGER ...]] [--dry-run] [--silent] \ [--singularity-cache SINGULARITY_CACHE] [--sif-cache SIF_CACHE] \ [--tmp-dir TMP_DIR] [--host-genome HOST_GENOME [HOST_GENOME ...]] \ [--threads THREADS] \ [--assembler ASSEMBLER] [--shallow-profile] \ [--workflow {pre-screen,read-based,assembly-based,combined}] \ --samplesheet SHEETPATH \ --output OUTPUT Optional arguments are shown in square brackets. A user must provide a sample sheet with --samplesheet and an output directory with --output . Use metamorph run -h to display the command-line help for this subcommand. 2.1 Required arguments ¶ Each of the following arguments is required. Failure to provide a required argument results in a non-zero exit code. --samplesheet SHEETPATH Full path to the delimited plain-text sample sheet. type: file The sample sheet is parsed before the pipeline is initialized. It must contain paths to the input DNA FASTQ files and can optionally contain a second column containing matching RNA FASTQ files. Example: --samplesheet /home/user/samplesheet.txt [!NOTE] Supported delimiters are inferred from the file extension: file extension delimiter *.txt tab *.tsv tab *.csv comma Supported sample sheet formats [!NOTE] Path = full absolute path to input FASTQ.GZ files R1 sample X / R2 sample X = paired-end read orientation n = total number of samples DNA only - 1 column: DNA ________ | DNA | |-------| R1 sample 1 | path | R2 sample 1 | path | ... | path | R1 sample n | path | R2 sample n | path | -------- DNA & RNA - 2 columns: DNA , RNA ________________ | DNA | RNA | |---------------| R1 sample 1 | path | path | R2 sample 1 | path | path | ... | path | path | R1 sample n | path | path | R2 sample n | path | path | ---------------- --output OUTPUT Path to an output directory. type: path This location is the pipeline working directory and is where metamorph creates its output files. If the directory does not exist, it is created automatically. Example: --output /data/$USER/metamorph_out 2.2 Analysis options ¶ Each of the following arguments is optional, and do not need to be provided. --workflow {pre-screen,read-based,assembly-based,combined} Select the analysis workflow. type: string default: pre-screen Available workflows: pre-screen : perform quality control, host-read removal, and run Centrifuger on dehosted reads. read-based : perform functional and taxonomic profiling on dehosted reads using HUMAnN3 and MetaPhlAn4. This stage follows pre-screening. assembly-based : perform the assembly and binning workflow on dehosted reads. This stage also follows pre-screening. combined : perform all steps included in the preceding modes. Example: --workflow combined --assembler ASSEMBLER Select the assembler(s) used by the assembly-based workflow. type: comma-separated string default: megahit,metaspades Supported assemblers are megahit and metaspades . One or both can be supplied. The command validates the comma-separated values after parsing and rejects unsupported assembler names. Examples: --assembler megahit,metaspades --assembler megahit --assembler metaspades --shallow-profile Use shallow HUMAnN3 profiling. type: boolean flag default: Runs translated protein search Disables the translated protein search of unaligned reads in HUMAnN3, which can significantly reduce runtime. Example: --shallow-profile --host-genome HOST_GENOME [HOST_GENOME ...] Screen out additional host/contaminant genome(s) during dehosting. type: one or more files default: none (dehosting only screens against the default host reference) Each dehosting step (DNA: bowtie2_dehost ) normally keeps a read pair if neither mate maps to the pipeline's default host reference. Supplying one or more FASTA files (optionally gzipped) here adds an additional screening pass: a read pair is only kept if neither mate maps to the default host reference or to any of these genomes. All genomes supplied are combined into one index, built once per run. This is useful for two different situations: confirming or ruling out that reads from a specific organism are being incorrectly removed as "host" during dehosting (supply that organism's genome and see whether real signal for it drops after dehosting), or dehosting against a non-human host entirely. Currently only wired into the DNA ( bowtie2_dehost ) dehosting step, not the RNA ( rna_dehost /STAR) step. Every dehosting pass (the default host-reference screen, and this one if used) writes a plain-text summary alongside the dehosted FASTQs: metagenome_results/trimmed_reads/{name}/{name}_hg38_dehost_summary.txt for the default screen, always; metagenome_results/trimmed_reads/{name}/{name}_injected_host_dehost_summary.txt for this screen, only when --host-genome is supplied. Each lists the reference/program used, the retention criterion, and the input/removed/retained read-pair counts and percentages for that sample. Example: --host-genome /data/$USER/refs/contaminant.fa 2.3 Orchestration options ¶ Each of the following arguments is optional. --mode {slurm,local} Select the execution method. type: string default: slurm Available modes: slurm : submits the pipeline and child jobs to the SLURM workload manager . It is recommended running metamorph in this mode as execution will be significantly faster in a distributed environment. This is the default mode of execution. local : run the pipeline locally on the current compute instance. This is useful for testing, debugging, or environments without a supported cluster job scheduler. Example: --mode slurm --job-name JOB_NAME Set the name of the pipeline master job. type: string default: pl:metamorph Overrides the default name used for the master job when the pipeline is submitted to a cluster job scheduler. By default, the name of the pipeline's master job is set to "pl:metamorph". Example: --job-name pl_id-2026-09-30 --master-job-node {norm,unlimited,quick} Select the node/partition class used for the master job. type: string default: unlimited The selected value is passed to the master-job submission wrapper as its job-node setting. Valid values are norm , unlimited , and quick . Example: --master-job-node norm --triggers TRIGGER [TRIGGER ...] Control Snakemake rerun triggers. type: zero or more validated strings default(in prority order): params,mtime,code,software-env,input Valid trigger names are: mtime code software-env input params Comma-separated trigger names are also accepted within a value, so both of the following forms are valid: --triggers mtime code --triggers mtime,code See the Snakemake command-line documentation for details about rerun triggers. Triggers are tied to the version of snakemake you are using. Example: --triggers mtime,code --dry-run Dry run the pipeline. type: boolean flag default: No dryrun is performed Displays the steps that remain or would be run without executing the workflow. Example: --dry-run --silent Silence standard output from master-job submission. type: boolean flag default: Standard output is more verbose Reduces the information written to standard output when the master job is submitted. In SLURM mode, only the master job ID is printed. Example: --silent --singularity-cache SINGULARITY_CACHE Override the Singularity cache directory. type: path default: <OUTPUT>/.singularity when no alternate cache is provided Singularity will cache image layers pulled from remote registries. This ultimately speeds up the process of pull an image from DockerHub if an image layer already exists in the singularity cache directory. By default, the cache is set to the value provided to the --output argument. Please note that this cache cannot be shared across users. Singularity strictly enforces you own the cache directory and will return a non-zero exit code if you do not own the cache directory! See the --sif-cache option to create a shareable resource. This part of the documentation describes options and concepts for metamorph unlock sub command in more detail. With minimal configuration, the unlock sub command enables you to unlock a pipeline output directory. If the pipeline fails ungracefully, it maybe required to unlock the working directory before proceeding again. Snakemake will inform a user when it maybe necessary to unlock a working directory with an error message stating: Error: Directory cannot be locked . Please verify that the pipeline is not running before running this command. If the pipeline is currently running, the workflow manager will report the working directory is locked. The is the default behavior of snakemake, and it is normal. Do NOT run this command if the pipeline is still running! Please kill the master job and it's child jobs prior to running this command. Unlocking metamorph pipeline output directory is fast and easy! In its most basic form, metamorph unlock only has one required input . 2. Synopsis ¶ $ ./metamorph unlock [-h] --output OUTPUT The synopsis for this command shows its parameters and their usage. Optional parameters are shown in square brackets. A user must provide an output directory to unlock via --output argument. After running the unlock sub command, you can resume the build or run pipeline from where it left off by re-running it. Use you can always use the -h option for information on a specific command. 2.1 Required Arguments ¶ --output OUTPUT Output directory to unlock. type: path Path to a previous run's output directory. This will remove a lock on the working directory. Please verify that the pipeline is not running before running this command. Example: --output /data/$USER/metamorph_out 2.2 Options ¶ Each of the following arguments are optional and do not need to be provided. -h, --help Display Help. type: boolean Shows command's synopsis, help message, and an example command Example: --help 3. docs.text: The metamorph executable is composed of several inter-related sub commands. Please see metamorph -h for all available options. This part of the documentation describes options and concepts for metamorph unlock sub command in more detail. With minimal configuration, the unlock sub command enables you to unlock a pipeline output directory. If the pipeline fails ungracefully, it maybe required to unlock the working directory before proceeding again. Snakemake will inform a user when it maybe necessary to unlock a working directory with an error message stating: Error: Directory cannot be locked . Please verify that the pipeline is not running before running this command. If the pipeline is currently running, the workflow manager will report the working directory is locked. The is the default behavior of snakemake, and it is normal. Do NOT run this command if the pipeline is still running! Please kill the master job and it's child jobs prior to running this command. Unlocking metamorph pipeline output directory is fast and easy! In its most basic form, metamorph unlock only has one required input .
docs.title: 1. About

docs.text: $ ./metamorph unlock [-h] --output OUTPUT The synopsis for this command shows its parameters and their usage. Optional parameters are shown in square brackets. A user must provide an output directory to unlock via --output argument. After running the unlock sub command, you can resume the build or run pipeline from where it left off by re-running it. Use you can always use the -h option for information on a specific command.
docs.title: 2. Synopsis

docs.text: --output OUTPUT Output directory to unlock. type: path Path to a previous run's output directory. This will remove a lock on the working directory. Please verify that the pipeline is not running before running this command. Example: --output /data/$USER/metamorph_out
docs.title: 2.1 Required Arguments

docs.text: Each of the following arguments are optional and do not need to be provided. -h, --help Display Help. type: boolean Shows command's synopsis, help message, and an example command Example: --help
